title: The switched bride (Genesis 29:21–30)
hookLine: the trickster is tricked, and wakes to find Leah instead of Rachel

cards: Seven years are up. Jacob goes to Laban: give me my wife, my time is done. Laban throws a great wedding feast and invites every man in the place.
There's food, there's drink. In the evening, Laban takes his daughter and brings her to Jacob. The Torah doesn't stop to explain how Jacob didn't know.
It just waits for daylight. And the next verse, in the old JPS translation, lands like a slap: "And it came to pass in the morning that, behold, it was Leah." Not Rachel.
Her older sister. After seven years of work, after all that love, Jacob wakes up to the wrong face. The trickster, tricked.

teach.b: Jacob storms to Laban: "What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?"
Laban answers, calm as anything: "It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the first-born."
The younger before the firstborn. That is exactly what Jacob did to Esau. Before a father whose eyes were too dim to see, Jacob, the younger, put himself in place of the firstborn.
Now, in the night, the firstborn is put in place of the younger, and Jacob is the one who can't see. A word ties the two stories together.
When Jacob asks why Laban beguiled him, the Hebrew is from the root of mirmah, deceit, the same root Isaac used to Esau: "Thy brother came with guile, and hath taken away thy blessing."
The Torah doesn't have to say it's payback. It just uses the same root. A midrash imagines the morning after.
Jacob says to Leah: all night I called you Rachel, and you answered. Leah says: your father called you Esau, and you answered.
The rabbis had a name for this pattern: measure for measure. What you do has a way of coming back around.

But notice Leah too, standing in the middle of two men's deals, married to someone who wanted her sister. Laban lets Jacob finish the wedding week, then gives him Rachel as well, for another seven years of work.
Jacob now has two wives, sisters, and a house built on a trick. Tomorrow, Leah's side.

how: Jews read the switched bride in the Torah portion Vayetze; one explanation given for the bedeken, when the groom lowers the bride's veil himself so he can see her face, points back to this story.

o: deceit, a trick played with guile
a curse a father lays on his son
a feast held to celebrate a wedding

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Jacob married only Rachel in the end
he married Leah first, then Rachel a week later, for seven more years of work.
the same Hebrew root for deceit appears in Jacob's story with Esau and with Laban
Isaac says, thy brother came with guile; Jacob asks Laban, why hast thou beguiled me?

games.q: you're Jacob. you wake up after your wedding night, and it's Leah, not Rachel. what does Laban tell you?
o: "it is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the first-born."
games.why: the younger before the firstborn: exactly what Jacob did to Esau. the trickster is tricked, measure for measure.

practice: Think of a time something you did came back to you, for better or worse: a shortcut that later cost you, a sharp word that returned in someone else's mouth, a kindness that came back years later from someone unexpected.
Stay with one, without judging it, and notice its shape: out, and back again. If you pray, you can ask to see your own part clearly.

wordCard.voice: Mirmah, Hebrew for deceit, the word that ties Jacob's trick on Esau to Laban's trick on Jacob.
